short.titel: ONE CALL, ONE PLANE: AMERICAN'S DC-3 DEAL
short.text:
One call wouldn't end until he said yes. American Airlines wanted a sleeper plane.

The caller was CEO C. R. Smith. Douglas Aircraft's founder, Donald Douglas, was reluctant.

The DC-2 cabin was only 66 inches wide. Too narrow for side-by-side berths.

So what changed his mind? Smith said American intended to buy 20 aircraft.

The sleeper prototype flew December 17, 1935, with a cabin 92 inches wide.

That call became the 21-seat DC-3. American's passenger service began June 26, 1936.

lang.titel: POKÉMON'S WORST NIGHT, AND HOW IT SURVIVED
lang.text:
Flashing red and blue lit up living rooms. Pokémon's cartoon went off the air after that night. But that wasn't the strangest part.

More than 10,000 viewers felt sick. They had sore eyes, headaches, dizziness and nausea. Hundreds of children were taken to hospitals. No one died.

This video answers one question. How did a game nobody expected much from become the world's estimated top-earning media franchise, and survive that night?

Be sure to like, share and save this video.

It starts with a boy hunting insects in ponds and fields near Tokyo. His name was Satoshi Tajiri. As Japan boomed, his town expanded, and its nature was largely destroyed.

Video games came next. An arcade opened in his neighborhood. At 17, he self-published a magazine called Game Freak. Magazines specializing in video games didn't yet exist in Japan.

Then Nintendo announced the Game Boy. Tajiri learned it would have a link port, so two machines could connect with a cable. Until then, that cable was only used for competing.

Then he remembered a Dragon Quest II item: an extremely rare hat. Tajiri never found one. Ken Sugimori, playing the same game, found two. That gave Tajiri an idea. A cable could transfer things between cartridges.

So Tajiri imagined catching creatures of differing rarity, then trading them with other players. He called it Capsule Monsters. But that name couldn't be trademarked, so it became Pocket Monsters, then Pokémon.

Tajiri pitched it at a company set up to give outsiders a chance. A Nintendo manager carried the idea to the president, who reportedly said, "This is the idea I've been waiting for."

A contract followed, but the budget was low. The game was meant to be small. Then the ideas grew, and the team realized it wouldn't be easy. The project was suspended indefinitely.

Years later, Tajiri decided to make a serious effort to finish it. New staff had joined. Atsuko Nishida created Pikachu. Producer Tsunekazu Ishihara added types and the Pokedex. Shigeru Miyamoto suggested two versions, each with creatures the other lacked. That pushed players to trade.

Then ownership got strange. Ishihara founded his own company, Creatures, which took co-ownership. Now three companies owned Pokémon: Game Freak, Creatures and Nintendo. One journalist called it probably the only such property in the world.

Tajiri and Ishihara once considered merging their companies. Tajiri refused. He said, "If Game Freak ceased to exist, then so would I."

The games launched to low expectations, and the media largely ignored them. The Game Boy was seven years old and considered dated. But it was everywhere, and cheap enough for children.

A children's magazine stepped in. One in four elementary school students read it. It ran a manga adaptation, then a contest for a secret creature called Mew. Twenty readers were chosen at random.

The lottery was a success and increased word of mouth. By September, sales had passed 1 million units. And the card game, released that October, became an instant success.

The cards were designed by Ishihara and three former colleagues, a simplified take on the first collectible card game ever. But in Japan that idea was new, and he struggled to find distributors.

Nintendo agreed to have them manufactured, but didn't want to build a distribution system. Then a small firm called Media Factory offered to distribute them.

Next came a fight over a cartoon. Nintendo hesitated, because a flop could hurt future games. Ishihara worried that people would assume Pokémon had ended when the series did.

Magazine editor Masakazu Kubo won everyone over. He promised the anime would last at least a year and a half, unusually long for a debut, and it needed a big investment.

Tajiri set one condition. Everyone on the anime team, even the voice actors, had to play the game extensively.

The team made Pikachu a central icon, expecting it to appeal to boys, girls and their mothers. Pikachu would only say its own name, in different tones. The show premiered in April 1997, and by November it topped TV Tokyo's ratings.

Then came the Porygon episode. The cast was chased through cyberspace by anti-virus missiles, and the explosions were bright, rapidly swapping red and blue flashes.

About 4.6 million households watched. Broadcasting was halted, and new guidelines were put in place to prevent a repeat. Meanwhile, the staff kept working on a feature film.

Yet the incident didn't damage the franchise. It grew during the hiatus. Rental tapes left shelves, but everything else kept selling. Businesses understood the anime was suspended, not canceled.

The anime returned in April 1998. The first film opened that July and became Japan's fourth highest-grossing film of the year.

Now came America. Nintendo of America's president Minoru Arakawa tried the game and thought it promising. His employees didn't believe it would work. Executives thought American children lacked the attention span for such a complex game.

They also feared it was too cute. So outside artists drew test designs: graffiti style, muscular creatures. Arakawa concluded it didn't work, and it was too late anyway.

Then market research came back negative. American kids reportedly didn't like Pokémon. Arakawa ignored the study and allocated a launch budget reportedly of at least $50 million, about equal to the Nintendo Entertainment System's launch budget.

Another obstacle: no national TV station wanted the show. 4Kids chief executive Alfred Kahn financed the production himself, knowing failure could bring down 4Kids.

So the show was offered free to local stations, in exchange for a share of advertising revenue. Nintendo of America also spent $5 million buying ad space on those stations. In the end, 112 broadcasters signed up, though often for early morning slots.

The marketing slogan was "Gotta catch 'em all." Normally the FCC prohibits commands in children's ads. But it reasoned that catching is at the core of play, so the phrase was allowed.

In the US, the anime was first broadcast on 7 September 1998. Three weeks later, Red and Blue arrived. By December, it was the highest-rated syndicated children's show on weekdays.

Warner Bros. then won a bidding war for the show. Its national debut was the most watched premiere in Kids' WB history.

Then shelves emptied. A toy store manager said 600 booster packs would last 24 hours. The card company said it had exhausted most of the card-printing capacity of the United States. Toy factories expanded production 20 times, and demand still exceeded supply.

In part because of the craze, Nintendo's profits rose 250% in 1999 compared with the year before.

So how did a game nobody expected much from get here? Not with one lucky break. Tajiri's cable idea became a trading game. A magazine contest spread the word. A risky cartoon survived its worst night. And a doubtful America got a huge launch bet.

Today the franchise is estimated to be the world's highest-grossing media franchise. Tajiri said the game represents the story of a boy's summer day.

If that surprised you, be sure to like, share and save this video.
